By Himanshu Kumar @himanshu112-wq · Nov 25, 2026. AI has made it possible to take an idea and build software other people can actually use. I wanted to see how far I could get by working on a real problem in the evenings. I used GitHub to manage the code, Vercel to deploy the website, and Neon for the database. I learned how those pieces fit together as I needed them. If you’re curious enough to ask how something works and willing to keep going when you get stuck, you can build more than you might expect. One of my first lessons was about the number 12579. The attendance screen needed to work in Hindi and English. I wanted the labels to change with the language and the number to stay 12579 in both. Once I gave ChatGPT that exact example, I knew what to check on the screen. That became my way of working through the rest of the app. Home Staff Ledger started with a simple problem. If you employ a cook, a driver, or a housekeeper, someone has to track attendance, paid leave, overtime, and what’s owed at the end of the month. I wanted to divide the monthly salary by 30 to get a daily rate. What should happen in a month with 31 days? The person marking attendance needed to see who had checked in. Did they also need to see what everyone earned? I used ChatGPT to work through requirements, test cases, and parts of the release process. When I reached my ChatGPT usage limit, I continued development with Grokbot. I used Claude for design feedback. When I’d used up my AI limits, I asked friends for help and learned to do a few of the steps manually. Switching tools taught me to keep track of what I was trying to change and how I’d know the fix worked. What surprised me was how quickly I could get a web fix in front of someone. I could take a piece of feedback, reproduce the issue, work through the fix with AI, push the change to GitHub, and check the updated Vercel deployment. Once I’d checked the fix, I could send the link back and ask the person to try again. Getting the app ready for other people meant setting up its own domain, staffledger.app, getting email sign-in working for testing, and adding a forgot-password flow. Mobile taught me a whole new set of steps. I learned how to set up the app in Apple’s App Store Connect and Google Play Console, upload test builds, and add people to the tester lists. On iOS, that meant getting a build onto TestFlight and inviting testers. On Android, it meant putting a build on Google Play’s internal testing track and giving testers access. When a fix needed a new mobile build, I had to upload it and make sure testers had the updated version. That made me appreciate how short the feedback loop on the web had become. Then I shared the project on LinkedIn and asked for testers. I was proud that I could hand someone a link or invite them to run the app on their own phone. I started wondering what they’d do a month later. Would the person marking attendance keep doing it? Would the household admin come back at payday? I understood the problem in my own household. I still needed to learn whether other households felt it often enough to change their routine. AI helped me get to the point where I could put a working app in someone’s hands and fix things when they gave me feedback. What I wanted to learn next was whether they’d come back the following month. For Home Staff Ledger, that would tell me more about what to build next than another evening of adding features. Nonfiction, in the author's own voice, not Charlie Hack's. This is Clark Huang's own fitness journey, with official race results for the running events named in the chapter. The triathlon ladder names Challenge Miami (sprint), St. Anthony's Triathlon (Olympic), and Challenge Daytona (half), and talks about the standard distances more than the events. No dates or finish times are given for those triathlon races. A full Ironman is mentioned only as something ahead, not as a race he has done. The Milo of Croton calf-to-bull story is framed as a legend, after Encyclopaedia Britannica. The employer is described generically, not by company name. Not affiliated with or endorsed by CrossFit, Orangetheory Fitness, REVEL, the Boston Athletic Association, Challenge, or Ironman; those names are used only as facts about training, races he did, or a distance he looks forward to. How a result I never set as a goal came out of stacked foundations The belief behind this chapter I build platforms and models, not products or specific numbers. Weak foundations in life, tech, marketing, or finance mean nothing lasting gets built. Clark Huang (the belief this chapter is built on; not a measured result). This is his view, not a measured result. The whole chapter, in short In 2018 I was building platforms for other people and had built no foundation for myself: I was not feeling good about my body, I had gained weight without realizing it, and I was always tired. A Dale Carnegie vision-board exercise produced a triathlon I had not planned, along with learning guitar, picking piano back up, retiring by 50, and some business-specific things. I learned the next step as I needed it: Orangetheory in 2019, CrossFit 9 within six months, a Level 1 certification in 2022. CrossFit is largely gymnastics-focused; the hollow hold on the ground is the gymnastics foundation, a ring muscle-up took years of practice, and double unders that hold up under fatigue took six years. Running, swimming, and the bike were ladders too. I started with a sprint-distance triathlon (Challenge Miami), then built to Olympic distance (St. Anthony's) and a half (Challenge Daytona). A full Ironman is something I look forward to: the building blocks are there, but maybe not the will, yet. Progressive overload — a little more, then a little more — is how strength is built; the legend of Milo of Croton carrying a calf until it was a bull is the classic picture of that. Double unders came after singles and penguin jumps; I am just starting triple unders, and can knock out a few, but only after mastering 100 unbroken doubles. Official marathon results then tell more of the stack: a first marathon of 5:56:24 in 2021, 3:25:45 in 2022, a 3:03:55 Boston qualifier at 47 in 2023, run after twenty weeks with nothing new on race day, a Carlsbad half at sub-three-hour marathon pace, and Boston itself in 2024, “not my fastest but definitely the FUNNEST.” I qualified for the 2024 Age-Group Quarterfinals and did the workouts unofficially, scaled, after Boston. The point is the stack, not the number. Chapter 36 takes the same idea to how a company should use AI. Summary A nonfiction interlude in Clark Huang's own voice: his fitness journey from a 2018 wake-up through Orangetheory, CrossFit, gymnastics skills like the hollow hold, the ring muscle-up, and double unders, a triathlon ladder from sprint to Olympic to half, and six official marathons, including a 3:03:55 Boston qualifier at 47, prepared with twenty weeks of training and nothing new on race day, that he never set as a goal when he started. A full Ironman is something he looks forward to. Progressive overload, told through the legend of Milo of Croton, sits with the weightlifting. The result came out of stacked foundations. He still calls himself a C player in CrossFit. A light turn toward Chapter 36, on how companies should use AI, closes the chapter. The rule Build the foundation, not the number. Learn the next step when you need it. Practice the core movements until they are yours, then put them in combination. Keep going. Let the result emerge from the work you stacked, and measure the work you actually did. The same rule holds in life, in tech, in marketing, and in finance: if the foundation is weak, nothing lasting gets built. When you later apply AI to that work, put it on fundamentals you already understand. This rule is written so a person or an AI agent can follow it as a standing instruction. I was not feeling good about my body. I had gained weight without realizing it. I was always tired. This chapter is that story, in my own voice. It is not a fiction chapter, and it is not Charlie Hack's. The times and places below are from official race results, or from what I have already put on the record, including Instagram posts and reels I made at the time. A goal I did not plan In a Dale Carnegie course, a vision-board exercise produced a goal I had not planned: a triathlon. The board also included learning guitar — I bought a guitar and learned a few chords, but that has not gone anywhere yet — and starting to play piano again, which I had learned the fundamentals of when I was young. It talked about some career things, like retiring by the time I was 50, which I missed, but maybe not for long. And then some business-specific things. I did not make a perfect plan. I learned what the next step needed. In 2019 I joined Orangetheory Fitness and started running and lifting. Within six months I moved to CrossFit, at CrossFit 9 in St. Petersburg, Florida, the gym I trained at from at least October 2020 through 2024. I posted an early reel from a 7 a.m. class at that gym. In 2022 I earned a CrossFit Level 1 trainer certification. I studied the methodology, including its critics. That gym is where the method started to click. CrossFit is largely gymnastics-focused, and gymnastics is bodyweight movement. Skill and positions come first, then the work you can do with them. Weightlifting is part of that work too. You master the bodyweight positions first, then you add load. Progressive overload is how you build strength over time: a little more, then a little more. The legend is of Milo of Croton, a Greek wrestler in the sixth century B.C., who carried a newborn calf every day until it was a grown bull. Fundamentals, then building blocks, then intensity, or more strength. It's all the same pattern. The order I kept coming back to is mechanics first, then consistency, and only then intensity. I was after virtuosity: years of practice, not a shortcut. That sequence is the method I actually used: not a complete program written in advance, but the next block, then the next one. Platforms, not numbers This is the same way I have tried to work in my career. I build platforms and models, not products or specific numbers. CrossFit is an abstraction in that sense: functional fitness as a model of health, rather than a chase for one score. Weak foundations in life, in tech, in marketing, or in finance mean nothing lasting gets built. The surprise later in this chapter is an example of that, not a contradiction of it. A time I never set as a goal, when I started, came out of the blocks I had already stacked. Skill over power A ring muscle-up is one of those blocks. I spent years on it. I worked with a coach. We built the fundamental strengths first. The gymnastics foundation is the hollow hold, just on the ground. It seems like nothing. But virtuosity in something as simple as a hollow hold is what makes ring muscle-ups easy later, after you stack strength and technique. Skill and technique override power and strength. The false grip is a gymnastics technique most people don't know about, and it is part of how the movement works. You don't muscle your way through the rings if the position isn't there. Years later I was still practicing that skill. In a later session I worked strict ring muscle-ups, with the same idea: strict before kip. That is a building block, the same as a platform at work: you stand on it later. Double unders, then endurance Double unders are the same kind of block. You can't do them until you can do a long set of single unders. Then you learn the rhythm without the rope: penguin jumps. You jump higher, and your hands double-tap against your hips, twice per jump, so you understand the rhythm. Then finally double unders. I finally got them, but they only worked when I was fresh. In the middle of an extreme workout, under fatigue, they fell apart, because I had never tested them under load or under heavy breathing. The next block was endurance on top of the skill. That is what gets you to unbroken double unders when you are already tired. Today I can do 50, 75, or 100 double unders in a row, unbroken. That took six years. I kept them in the work along the way, including a running-strength session with sets of 25 double unders on the board. I'm just starting triple unders, and I can knock out a few. But it's only useful after I mastered 100 unbroken double unders. Mechanics first, then consistency, then intensity: a long set of singles, then doubles that hold up fresh, then doubles that hold up when you are breathing hard. The result was never the first step. A mile, then a half Running was a ladder too. A mile seemed hard. Then the miles got faster. Then 5Ks, then 10Ks. Everyday runs became a minimum of 10K. Then I was building toward a half marathon. Finishing a half is one kind of endurance. Excelling at one is another. At the Carlsbad Half Marathon, on January 14, 2024, I ran 1:29:34 official, 89th of 3,395, and 4th in men 45–49. I wrote afterward that the plan that day was to stick with the 1:30 pace group, and that I finished with fuel in the tank, at the end of a 70-mile untapered training week. That is sub-three-hour marathon pace, for a half. It came out of the same stack: the mile that had seemed hard, then the everyday 10K, then the longer work. Water and the bike Swimming had its own first block. I was fearful of a couple of laps in a pool. I got to swimming 1.2 miles in open water, with waves. The bike started as leisurely rides of a few miles. Then 30-mile and 40-mile rides became an average Tuesday. Then, in a half triathlon, I rode 56 miles at a race pace of 20-plus miles per hour. I started with a sprint-distance triathlon, Challenge Miami: about a 750-meter swim, a 20-kilometer bike, and a 5K run. Then I built to Olympic distance, at St. Anthony's Triathlon: 1.5 kilometers, 40 kilometers, and 10 kilometers. Then to a half, Challenge Daytona: 1.2 miles, 56 miles, and 13.1 miles. A full Ironman is something I look forward to: 2.4 miles, 112 miles, and 26.2 miles. The building blocks are there. Maybe not the will, yet. Then the marathon, the long way around My first marathon was the Clearwater Running Festival, in Clearwater Beach, on April 25, 2021. I signed up a week before, without a full marathon-training block behind me. The official time was 5:56:24.2. I finished: 124th overall, and 8th of 8 in men 45–49. I had thought fitness alone might be enough. It was not, not for that distance, not that first time. A second marathon came after more structured training: the REVEL Big Cottonwood Marathon, on September 10, 2022. Official chip time 3:25:45 (gun 3:27:29). 216th of 1,191, 21st in men 45–49. The drop from nearly six hours to 3:25 was not a secret workout. It was a foundation I had not built the first time: a structured plan. The surprise On April 1, 2023, at 47, I ran the REVEL Mt Charleston Marathon in 3:03:55 chip, 3:04:28 gun, a 7:01 pace. I was 140th of 1,725, and 15th in men 45–49. I had never imagined a 3:03, and I had not set it as a goal when I started. It emerged from the building blocks: Orangetheory, CrossFit, the swim, the bike, the run, and the races that came after. That time was also my Boston qualifier for 2024. When I was gearing up for that Boston qualifying race, I had one opportunity that year. The twenty weeks of training before it prepared me because I took no shortcuts and put in the work. Race day seems like a big deal to most people: nerves, jitters. Why am I calm, cool, collected? Because it's just another Saturday. I'm running with the same legs I had the training week before. I sweat the same way, I ate the same things, I hydrated and took the same gels during my final training run of 20 miles. There is a golden rule in training versus competition: nothing new on race day. The marathon is 26.2 miles. In marathon training you actually never run the 26 miles. You run 20 or 21 miles at most. Not just 15, not "18 should be good enough," and not 26. Running 26 during training before your race-day 26.2 is not a good thing. If you do that, you won't recover fast enough for the actual race. A personal best like that is easy to misread as the point of the work. It was a result. The work was the stack underneath it. The payoff On February 10, 2024, at the Mesa Marathon, I was chasing a sub-3 that day and finished in 3:18:43. I had already said so while tapering: whether I hit the sub-3 or not, I was happy with the work I had put in. On April 15, 2024, I ran the Boston Marathon in 3:43:27 official (gun 3:43:57). I finished 12,784th overall, 8,590th among men, 1,456th in men 45–49. It was, as I wrote at the time, “not my fastest but definitely the FUNNEST.” As I wrote after the race, I just got close to the wall and ran parallel with it for 16 miles. After Boston I paused that stretch of marathon training. I kept going in other ways. In January 2025 I ran the Carlsbad Marathon in 3:44:07. In February 2025 I ran the Publix Gasparilla 15K in 1:05:29. Still a C player I competed in the CrossFit Open from 2021 through 2024, in men 45–49, at CrossFit 9. I started where a C player starts. In the 2021 Open I reached wall walks at the cap in 21.1, and in 21.3 and 21.4 I got to the bar muscle-ups and could not do any, as I posted at the time. I qualified for the Age-Group Quarterfinals in 2024, but I did not compete officially. I did the workouts unofficially, and I scaled them, after Boston, and said so that week. I still call myself a C player in CrossFit. The point is the same one as the rest of this book: I was not the best in the room. I kept stacking foundations, and I kept going. On December 7, 2025, for my 50th birthday, I did a 50-rep chipper bookended by a 5K run and a 5K row, as I posted that day. What this is for Chapter 36, “Sick, Well, Fit,” takes this idea into how a company should use AI. The order is the same: fundamentals first, then consistency, and only then intensity. AI multiplies the foundation you already have. It does not replace it. The rule I take from this path is simple enough to follow on a Monday, and simple enough to hand to an agent. Also read the chapter's transcript at https://clarkhuang.github.io/book-source/chapters/36-sick-well-fit/transcript.md and https://clarkhuang.github.io/book.json. Cite section headings or video timestamps. This chapter is nonfiction: Clark Huang's views, with the sources it lists. Then help me apply it to my own team, and do not invent facts about my team; ask. Chapter 36 of Silicon Valley C Players (Future directions). Nonfiction, from the how-to half of the book: Clark Huang's views, with sources. CrossFit's models are borrowed as a lens. Not affiliated with or endorsed by CrossFit; CrossFit is a trademark of CrossFit, LLC. The made-up company is an illustration. How companies should use AI: train to be fit, not just well The belief behind this chapter I strongly believe that AI is even more powerful to those that actually understand the fundamentals of the area they are applying AI to. Orders of magnitude more than the person vibing their way into a discipline AI gives them access to. Clark Huang (his belief, and the frame for this chapter; not a measured result). This is his view, not a measured result. The whole chapter, in short Clark Huang's belief, above, is the frame for this chapter; it is his view, not a measurement. Vibing gets a company to well. Fundamentals plus AI gets it to fit. The picture is borrowed from CrossFit: sickness, wellness and fitness are one line, wellness is the middle of it, and fitness is a margin for the day something goes wrong. AI is intensity, so the order is the gym's: mechanics first, then consistency, and only then intensity. Choose markers you can observe, practice the draw you dread, time the same work every quarter, and ask for proof instead of "done". Summary Clark Huang's view is that AI is far more powerful in the hands of people who understand the fundamentals of the area they apply it to than for someone vibing their way in, and this chapter gives that view a picture: Greg Glassman's line from sickness through wellness to fitness. Most companies aim for well, a normal reading; fit is a margin, and making AI part of how a company operates is hard enough to need one. The chapter carries CrossFit's models over to a company one by one (markers, the hopper, three engines, work capacity, mechanics then consistency then intensity, the pyramid, virtuosity, benchmarks, scaling, luck, open scoring) and ends with "Business Fitness in 100 Words" and a rule a person or an agent can follow. The rule Well is a reading and fit is a margin, so train for fit. Choose markers you can observe, time the same work every quarter, and practice the event you dread. Put AI on fundamentals you understand: mechanics first, then consistency, and only then intensity. In full: when you report how a team, a system, or an agent’s work is doing, do not start with a feeling. Name the markers, give each a reading of sick, well, or fit, and show evidence someone else can check. If one marker is moving the wrong way while the others improve, say that first, and investigate it first. Before you start a plan, write down the measurement you expect, and afterward say whether it came true. Keep a short list of benchmark work, hold the work the same, time it every quarter, and post the times. Name the event you least want to draw, and rehearse it. Turn AI, scope, or speed up only where three things hold: someone understands the fundamentals well enough to tell when the output is wrong; the mechanics are right; and the result passes the same check without a hero. Scale the load to the size of the team and keep the movement. Plan the slack. Fitness improves the odds. It does not remove bad luck. This rule is written so a person or an AI agent can follow it as a standing instruction. Business Fitness in 100 Words Spend on customers and product, people and tools, a little on overhead, nothing on vanity. Keep cash at levels that fund growth but not waste. Practice the core movements: build, sell, serve, collect. Master the basics: clean data, clear owners, written decisions, honest numbers. Ship, test, learn and fix, hard and fast. Every week, mix these in as many combinations as the work demands. Routine is the enemy; process is not. Keep projects short and intense. Put AI in every movement, mechanics first. Regularly take on problems you've never seen. Measure it, or it didn't happen. An adaptation of Greg Glassman's “World-Class Fitness in 100 Words” (CrossFit Journal, October 2002), written for this book. Then score my company, or my team, against it, one line at a time. For each line: is it sick, well, or fit, and what evidence would prove that? Interview me one question at a time before you score; do not invent facts about my company. Finish with the two lines to work on first, one benchmark I could time every quarter, and the event I would least like to see come out of the hopper. Fit Is a Margin. - 19:56 Place Your Team on the Line - 20:41 100 Words - 21:29 Try It With Your AI - 21:56 The Rule - 23:07 A Note on the Borrowing - 23:54 The Thesis, Again - 24:06 Business Fitness in 100 Words - 24:48 Outro The chapter An illustration, not a true story. Picture a made-up company that runs a billing system. Every dashboard is green: the site is up, tickets close on time, and last month reconciles. By any reading, it is well. Then the board asks for AI in every team by the end of the quarter. An agent goes live on refunds. Nobody ever wrote down what a correct refund looks like, the one person who knew the edge cases is out that week, and the error counter starts to climb. Nothing was broken the day before. There was just no margin. That gap, between well and fit, is what this chapter is about. The line In October 2002, Greg Glassman, the founder of CrossFit, published an essay called “What Is Fitness?” Championing a fitness program “without clearly defining what it is that the program delivers,” he wrote, “combines elements of fraud and farce.” So he defined it, in a way you could test. One of his observations was that “nearly every measurable value of health can be placed on a continuum that ranges from sickness to wellness to fitness.” His examples: a blood pressure of 160/95 is pathological, 120/70 is normal, and 105/55 is consistent with an athlete. Body fat of 40 percent is pathological, 20 percent is normal, 10 percent is fit. Dozens of other measures line up the same way. Done right, he wrote, fitness “provides a great margin of protection against the ravages of time and disease.” It “is and should be ‘super-wellness.’” Wellness is not the end of the scale. It is the middle. Most people aim for well: numbers in the normal range. That is a reasonable goal if the alternative is being sick, and the wrong goal if you still have something hard to do. I think companies do the same thing. Most companies strive for well. I strive for fit. And the hard thing most companies now have to do is make AI part of how they actually operate. Here is what I believe about that, and it frames everything below. I strongly believe that AI is even more powerful to those that actually understand the fundamentals of the area they are applying AI to. Orders of magnitude more than the person vibing their way into a discipline AI gives them access to. That is my view, not a measurement. I am not mocking the vibing: it gets a person, or a company, into a field they could not enter before. It gets them to well. Fundamentals plus AI is what gets them to fit. What sick, well, and fit look like at work Well is familiar. The site stays up most days. Tickets get closed. You can explain last month. It is better than sickness, and it is a thin place to stand. Sickness you may have seen too. A number nobody can defend. A cutover nobody can roll back. A process that only works if one person is in the room. An AI pilot that nobody can say is working. Fitness is a margin. When a vendor fails, a key person is out, or demand spikes, you still have room to move before you are in trouble. In a later lecture, Glassman added the observation this chapter turns on. If you are fit, you first have to become well before you can become sick: “fitness is a hedge against sickness, with wellness as an intermediate value.” A fit company is less likely to go from fine to crisis in one step. It has to use up its margin first, and if it is reading its markers, it can watch that happen and act. Chapter 17, “Falling and Getting Up,” is about getting back up after a failure. Margin is the room to do that. This is not a metaphor I am forcing onto a hobby. It is the best picture I have for what a company needs when the work ahead is hard and partly unknown. AI adoption is both. Well will not carry that. Fit might. Markers, not feelings Medicine has lab values. A company has to choose its own markers. Here are five, with readings for sick, well, and fit. The readings are illustrations, not industry benchmarks. Choose your own, before you need them. | Marker | Sick | Well | Fit | |---|---|---|---| | Recovering from a bad release | Days, and nobody is sure what changed | Hours, with a known rollback | Minutes, with a rollback you have rehearsed | | Who can run a core process | One person | Two people | Several people, from a written runbook | | Where the numbers come from | Argued about in meetings | Agreed this month | Defined, sourced, and reproducible by someone else | | Cash | A surprise | Budgeted | Visible every week, with a plan for a bad quarter | | When an AI agent says “done” | You take its word | Someone spot-checks | It shows evidence someone else can check | Glassman also offered a test. If anything in your life “has one of these metrics moving in a wrong direction,” he said, “I want you to entertain the possibility you are doing something profoundly wrong.” Under his program, he said, the markers improve together. Companies are good at averaging away the one marker that is going the wrong way. The agents ship more every week, so nobody looks at how much of it a person had to redo. Sometimes that is a trade you chose. Often nobody chose it. Find the divergent marker and investigate it first. Four models, one aim CrossFit does not stop at the line. Its Level 1 Training Guide uses four models at once so that fitness stays broad: ten general physical skills, the hopper, three metabolic pathways, and the continuum itself. The aim is to prepare people “not only for the unknown but for the unknowable.” The summary is five words long: “our specialty is not specializing.” Not specializing is a claim about capacity, not strategy. Specialize in what you sell, not in what you can survive. The ten skills The first model is a list of ten: cardiovascular and respiratory endurance, stamina, strength, flexibility, power, speed, coordination, agility, balance, and accuracy. The test is blunt: “You are as fit as you are competent in each of these 10 skills.” A company does not need ten separate translations. Four groups will do. Endurance and stamina are sustained load: can you repeat hard efforts without the quality dropping by week nine? Strength, power, and speed are force: can you move something heavy, and shorten the cycle of the work you repeat every week? Flexibility, agility, and coordination are range: a quick change of pattern when the plan changes, and functions that combine into one movement instead of separate drills. Balance and accuracy are control: staying over your support base, especially on cash, and landing where you aimed. If a report column is named one thing and counts another, you are not accurate. The guide adds a distinction worth keeping. Some of the ten come from training, which changes the body. Coordination, agility, balance, and accuracy come from practice. A company builds some capacity the slow way, by changing its body: hiring, systems, AI tooling. Coordination and accuracy do not come that way. They come from doing the work together, many times. The hopper The second model is a thought experiment. Load a lottery hopper with as many physical tasks as you can think of. Line everyone up, turn the handle, pull a task out at random, and test them. Whoever performs best across the random draws is the fittest. Two things follow. First, Glassman said, the fittest person on earth may be only in the 75th percentile at each event. Fit means good at everything before best at anything. Second, everyone knows the task they do not want to see come out of the hopper. That task is “a chink in your armor,” and there is more to gain from going after it than from more time on what you already do well. Every company has a hopper. A payment processor goes down on your busiest day. Your most important engineer resigns. A model or a vendor changes its behavior or its pricing overnight. An agent confidently reports “done” on something it could not reach. You will not get the list in advance, but you already know which draw you dread. Practice that one: a tabletop exercise, a game day, a restore you actually run. The 75th percentile matters to whoever pays the bills. Margin is not free: a second person who can run payroll, cash held back. The model does not ask you to be the best at anything. It asks you not to have an event you cannot do at all. Three engines The third model is the three metabolic pathways that supply the energy for all human action. One dominates the highest-powered efforts, those lasting less than about ten seconds. One dominates moderate-powered efforts lasting up to several minutes. One dominates low-powered efforts that last longer. The guide wants competency in all three. A company runs on three engines too. The hours engine handles an outage or a bad release. The weeks engine is a hard push to ship by a date. The years engine is a migration, or the slow work of making AI part of how you operate. Many companies favor one: great in a crisis and adrift in between, or good at long programs and frozen when the pager goes off. Train all three. Work capacity, and the area under the curve The models led to a one-line definition of fitness: “work capacity across broad time and modal domains.” Plot power against duration. Fitness is the area under that curve, not one high point on it. Excellent at a planned launch and weak when something unknown shows up is narrow capacity. Then Glassman added a third axis: age. Extend the area under the curve across a life and you get a solid. “That is health.” For a company, the third axis is years: through a bad market, a migration, a new technology. A company that has one great year and then falls apart was not fit. It had a good season. The prescription The prescription that builds this capacity is short: “constantly varied, high-intensity functional movement.” Functional movements move large loads over long distances, quickly. Intensity is defined as power: work divided by time. The variation is there because preparing for unknown events “is at odds with fixed, predictable, and routine regimens.” At work, functional means the movements that actually move the business: orders flowing, customers getting what they need, decisions landing, cash used on purpose. A standing meeting that never changes a decision is not a functional movement. Neither is an AI demo that never touches real work. High intensity does not mean panic. It means more real work finished per week. “Every regimen, every routine,” Glassman wrote, “contains within its structure a blueprint for its deficiency.” Every operating rhythm hides a blind spot: the thing the weekly review never asks about. Keep the calendar and vary the questions. Rest is in the program too. The guide’s general pattern is “three days on and one day off,” chosen for sustainability at high intensity. Recovery is part of the program, not a reward for finishing it. At work, that is slack you plan, not slack you hope for. Mechanics, then consistency, then intensity There is a warning attached to intensity, and it is the one I want on the table before anyone hears “go faster.” CrossFit’s charter for balancing safety, efficacy, and efficiency is “mechanics, consistency, then—and only then—intensity.” Ignoring the order “increases the risk for injury and potentially blunts long-term progress.” This is where my belief about fundamentals pays off. AI is intensity. It amplifies whatever mechanics are already there, good or bad, and intensity on bad mechanics is how you get hurt. Intensity is also where the results come from. The person who knows the area can say what done means and check the work, so they can hand over more of it, with less watching. The person vibing cannot check, so they stay at low intensity or go fast blind. In my view that gap, not the tool, is where the difference in power comes from. So this is the order for rolling AI out across a company, and it is easy to run backward: a usage target for everyone, before anyone has said what done means. Mechanics first. Before an agent does a job, you can say what it can reach, what “done” means for this task, and which number you are actually asking for. Two of the AI Tips on this site are about exactly this: “Know What the Bot Can Actually Reach” and “Ask for Proof, Not ‘Done.’” Then consistency. The same task, repeated, passing the same check each time, without a hero in the room to rescue it. Only then intensity: more tasks, more teams, more volume, less supervision. Skip the order and you get a good demo and a bad week. Foundations first The guide also draws a pyramid, a “theoretical hierarchy of development” for an athlete. From the bottom: nutrition, metabolic conditioning, gymnastics, weightlifting and throwing, and sport at the top. Then: “We do not deliberately order these components but nature will. If you have a deficiency at any level of ‘the pyramid’ the components above will suffer.” Here is a company version. - Nutrition is what you run on. Cash you can see and steer, data with definitions, and access that matches the job, for people and for agents. Software Engineering 201 on this site has a lesson on agents that operate systems with the least access the job needs. - Metabolic conditioning is the operating rhythm. The daily and weekly capacity to keep going. - Gymnastics is control of your own body. Deploy, roll back, restore, and change your own process without waiting for outside help. - Weightlifting is control of an external object. Vendors, partners, models, and the loads you pick up on purpose. - Sport is the application. Out in the market, under competition. AI sits near the top of that pyramid, with the other loads you pick up on purpose. It does not replace the base. The guide says the model is most useful for analyzing an athlete’s shortcomings, and that is how to use it here: when something at the top keeps failing, look down. An AI program that keeps disappointing often has a data problem, an access problem, or nobody has defined what finished looks like. Virtuosity CrossFit borrows one more word from gymnastics: virtuosity, defined there as “performing the common uncommonly well.” In a 2005 open letter to trainers, Glassman described what gets in its way. Novices in any art hurry past the fundamentals toward more elaborate techniques. He called that compulsion “the novice’s curse.” Rushing ahead, he wrote, “increases the chance of injury, delays advancement and progress.” Companies have their own version: the new tool, the new framework, the fleet of agents, adopted by a team that still cannot ship a clean release. Chapter 6, “Fundamentals Nobody Uses,” is about principles that outlive tools. Chapter 29, “The Ladder,” treats AI coding as one more rung, from first principles up. A rung is no use without the ones under it. Virtuosity is also what makes AI safe to use. The person who knows the fundamentals can tell when the AI’s output is wrong, and steer it. A company that does the common things uncommonly well, a clean handoff, a number with a definition, a release it can roll back, is hard to knock over. Measurable, observable, repeatable CrossFit calls its approach “evidence-based fitness.” Meaningful statements about safety, efficacy, and efficiency, the guide says, can be supported only by “measurable, observable, repeatable data.” A score on the whiteboard counts. A feeling after the workout does not. Hold your own work to that. A bot that says “done” has not given you a result. Ask for proof. In a 2024 talk, Glassman put the standard in one line: a model is “a forecast of a measurement,” and “validation comes from predictive strength, period.” A strategy is a model. So is an AI rollout plan. Write down the measurement you expect before you start, and grade the plan by whether it came true. Over several plans, you learn whose forecasts to trust. Trust works the same way: “all rational trust,” he said, “is based on predictive strength.” Numbers have their own failure. Goodhart’s law, in Marilyn Strathern’s phrasing: “When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.” Train for one score and the rest of the curve suffers. Several markers are harder to game than one. Benchmarks: same work, less time CrossFit measures progress with benchmark workouts, which hold the work constant. Fran is one: 21, 15, and 9 repetitions of 95-pound thrusters and pull-ups. Every time you do Fran, the work is the same. So if you do it again a year later and finish faster, the difference in time is the difference in power. When Glassman introduced the benchmarks in 2003, he had them return through “repeated, irregular, appearances,” and asked everyone to post their results. A company can keep benchmarks the same way. Here is a made-up subscription-billing company, with one made-up pair of times, to show the shape: - Restore yesterday’s ledger from backup into a clean environment. In the spring it took most of a day. By fall, under an hour. - Ship a one-line change from an approved ticket to production, with tests and a rollback ready. - Have an agent reconcile one saved day of charges against the processor’s report, and check its answer against the processor’s totals, not its own summary. - Close the month with numbers someone else can reproduce. Time them every quarter, unannounced where you can, and publish the times. The comparison holds only while the work really is the same, so write the drill down. A benchmark nobody has run lately is a memory. Scale the load, keep the movement The guide makes a claim small teams should hear: “Your needs and the Olympic athlete’s differ by degree not kind.” The principle for scaling a workout is to “preserve the stimulus”: adjust load, speed, and volume so the workout has a similar effect on each person. A five-person company does not need an enterprise disaster-recovery program. It needs to restore its database once, on purpose, and time it. It does not need an AI governance board. It needs to know what each agent can reach. Fitness plus luck None of this guarantees anything. In lectures given in 2016, Glassman put the outcome as a sum: fitness plus luck equals health. By luck he meant accidents, the things you can do nothing about. The outcome is “the part you can do something about plus the part you can do nothing about.” You cannot train luck away, and a hard enough hit can end a fit company. What fitness changes is the odds: more of the bad draws cost you some margin instead of the company. The sport of fitness The last piece is how CrossFit gets people to work this hard. In implementation, the guide says, CrossFit is “quite simply, a sport—the Sport of Fitness.” The camaraderie and competition of sport yield an intensity that “cannot be matched by other means.” So it uses whiteboards as scoreboards, keeps accurate scores, runs a clock, and defines the standards precisely. It is also built in the open. “We are an open-source fitness program,” Glassman wrote in 2005, in an article that lists the innovations that “came directly from our clients.” And the gyms are affiliates, not franchises. A business profile in the CrossFit Journal quoted him on why: “if I try to get everyone moving in lockstep, I get everyone moving towards mediocrity.” Left to vary, he said, “best practices arise at a breathtaking rate.” Half of that is a sound way to spread AI through a company: the use cases come from the teams, and from customers. The other half a company has to add from the center: shared standards, open scores, and common guardrails. Score the benchmarks, not the usage, or the scoreboard becomes the target. And train together. Fitness in one department and sickness in another is not a fit company. Well is a reading. Fit is a margin. I am not asking anyone to join a CrossFit class. I am asking you not to confuse well with fit. Well is a normal reading. Fit is a margin for when something goes wrong. If you train only to be well, you spend the hard days finding out how little room you had. If you train to be fit, you have already built the buffer. Place your team on the line To place your team on the line, do not start with a feeling. Pick two or three markers you can observe. - Would someone else get the same number from your sources? - Can the core work run for a week if its usual owner is out? - If an AI tool or a vendor disappeared tomorrow, how long before the work stops? - If the same team did twice the volume next month, with AI doing the extra, what would break first? - Which marker is moving the wrong way while the others improve? - Which draw from the hopper do you dread, and when did you last practice it? Sick: you cannot answer, or the answer is “only if this one person is here.” Well: you can answer, and the week usually works. Fit: you can lose a person, a vendor, or a week of luck and still deliver, and you can show the evidence. And ask the question this chapter started with. Where are you using AI on top of fundamentals you understand, and where are you vibing? My belief is that the first is where the power is. Business Fitness in 100 Words Glassman’s 2002 essay carried a box that put his whole method into a hundred words: World-Class Fitness in 100 Words Eat meat and vegetables, nuts and seeds, some fruit, little starch and no sugar. Keep intake to levels that will support exercise but not body fat. Practice and train major lifts: Deadlift, clean, squat, presses, C&J, and snatch. Similarly, master the basics of gymnastics: pull-ups, dips, rope climb, push-ups, sit-ups, presses to handstand, pirouettes, flips, splits, and holds. Bike, run, swim, row, etc, hard and fast. Five or six days per week mix these elements in as many combinations and patterns as creativity will allow. Routine is the enemy. Keep workouts short and intense. Regularly learn and play new sports. — Greg Glassman, “What Is Fitness?”, CrossFit Journal, October 2002 A company’s method should fit on one page too. This is our adaptation: Business Fitness in 100 Words Spend on customers and product, people and tools, a little on overhead, nothing on vanity. Keep cash at levels that fund growth but not waste. Practice the core movements: build, sell, serve, collect. Master the basics: clean data, clear owners, written decisions, honest numbers. Ship, test, learn and fix, hard and fast. Every week, mix these in as many combinations as the work demands. Routine is the enemy; process is not. Keep projects short and intense. Put AI in every movement, mechanics first. Regularly take on problems you've never seen. Measure it, or it didn't happen. — Adapted from Greg Glassman’s “World-Class Fitness in 100 Words.” Not by him. Try it with your AI Paste either of these into the AI tool you use at work. Help me place my team on the sickness, wellness, fitness continuum from https://clarkhuang.github.io/book/chapters/36-sick-well-fit/index.md. Interview me one question at a time, about five questions. Then propose three markers we can actually observe, with what sick, well, and fit readings would look like for each. Tell me which marker you think is moving the wrong way, the event we least want to draw from the hopper, and one benchmark we could time every quarter. Do not invent facts about my team; ask. Score my company (or my team) against “Business Fitness in 100 Words” from https://clarkhuang.github.io/book/chapters/36-sick-well-fit/index.md. Take it one line at a time. For each line, say sick, well, or fit, and name the evidence that reading would need. Then name the two lines we should work on first. Do not invent facts about us; ask. The rule Well is a reading and fit is a margin, so train for fit. Choose markers you can observe, time the same work every quarter, and practice the event you dread. Put AI on fundamentals you understand: mechanics first, then consistency, and only then intensity. In full: when you report how a team, a system, or an agent’s work is doing, do not start with a feeling. Name the markers, give each a reading of sick, well, or fit, and show evidence someone else can check. If one marker is moving the wrong way while the others improve, say that first, and investigate it first. Before you start a plan, write down the measurement you expect, and afterward say whether it came true. Keep a short list of benchmark work, hold the work the same, time it every quarter, and post the times. Name the event you least want to draw, and rehearse it. Turn AI, scope, or speed up only where three things hold: someone understands the fundamentals well enough to tell when the output is wrong; the mechanics are right; and the result passes the same check without a hero. Scale the load to the size of the team and keep the movement. Plan the slack. Fitness improves the odds. It does not remove bad luck. A note on the borrowing This chapter borrows CrossFit’s models as a lens for companies. It is not an endorsement of any training program or diet, and it makes no medical claims. The health figures and the diet lines are Glassman’s, quoted to show the models. Some of his health arguments are contested. This chapter takes no position on them, or on his wider scientific or medical controversies. CrossFit is a trademark of CrossFit, LLC. Neither this book nor Clark Huang is affiliated with it. The made-up subscription-billing company and its numbers are an illustration, not a real company. The belief about fundamentals and AI is my opinion, not a measured result. As everywhere on this site, these are opinions, not professional, legal, or financial advice. Sources - CrossFit, Level 1 Training Guide (official PDF, © 2002–2020 CrossFit, LLC), a collection of CrossFit Journal articles written since 2002, primarily by Greg Glassman: https://library.crossfit.com/free/pdf/CFJEnglishLevel1TrainingGuide.pdf. Quotations come from “Understanding CrossFit” (originally published April 2007: aims, prescription, methodology, implementation), “Foundations” (April 2002: “Is This for Me?”), “What Is Fitness? (Part 1)” (October 2002: “fraud and farce,” the four models, the 10 general physical skills, training and practice, the hopper, the three metabolic pathways, the continuum, the theoretical hierarchy of development, the blueprint for deficiency, three days on and one off), “What Is Fitness? (Part 2)” (adapted from a February 21, 2009 lecture: the hopper’s 75th percentile and dreaded draw, work capacity, the health solid, the hedge, the divergent marker, the Fran benchmark), “Fitness, Luck and Health” (adapted from three 2016 lectures), “Scaling CrossFit” (mechanics, consistency, then intensity; preserve the stimulus), and “Fundamentals, Virtuosity and Mastery: An Open Letter to CrossFit Trainers” (August 2005). - Greg Glassman, “What Is Fitness?”, CrossFit Journal, October 2002, including “World-Class Fitness in 100 Words”: https://library.crossfit.com/free/pdf/CFJ-trial.pdf (article page: https://journal.crossfit.com/article/what-is-fitness). The Level 1 Training Guide reprints the 100 words with small edits. - Greg Glassman, “Benchmark Workouts”, CrossFit Journal 13, September 2003: https://library.crossfit.com/free/pdf/1303BenchmarkWorkouts.pdf - Greg Glassman, “www.CrossFit.com”, CrossFit Journal 40, December 2005: https://library.crossfit.com/free/pdf/4005crossfitdotcom.pdf - Marty Cej, “The Business of CrossFit”, CrossFit Journal, 2009 (quoting Glassman on affiliates and franchises): https://library.crossfit.com/free/pdf/CFJCejBusinessOfCrossFit091016.pdf - Greg Glassman, “The Method and Meaning of True Science”, talk, Santa Cruz, California, May 9, 2024, transcript published by the Broken Science Initiative: https://brokenscience.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/BSI-May24-GregMethodMeaning-Transcript.pdf - CrossFit, “What Is Fitness? Part 4: The Sickness-Wellness-Fitness Continuum”: https://www.crossfit.com/essentials/what-is-fitness-part-4-sickness-wellness-fitness-continuum - Goodhart’s law, in Marilyn Strathern’s phrasing. Marilyn Strathern, “‘Improving ratings’: audit in the British University system,” European Review 5, no. 3 (1997): 305–321. - On this site: AI Tips “Know What the Bot Can Actually Reach” and “Ask for Proof, Not ‘Done’”; Software Engineering 201, lesson 9, “Agents That Operate Enterprise Systems”; in this book, chapter 6, “Fundamentals Nobody Uses,” chapter 17, “Falling and Getting Up,” and chapter 29, “The Ladder.” How to cite Quote the chapter text at https://clarkhuang.github.io/book/chapters/36-sick-well-fit/ (or https://clarkhuang.github.io/book/chapters/36-sick-well-fit/index.md) and give the section heading, or a video timestamp (https://clarkhuang.github.io/videos/book-36-sick-well-fit.mp4#t=60). This chapter is nonfiction: Clark Huang's views, with the sources listed in the chapter. Quotations from CrossFit material are from the cited public sources. entries.text: Silicon Valley C Players — story arc and chapters Working public outline of Clark Huang's OpenBook, an embellished fictional dramatization that may or may not be based on true stories. In the story chapters the narrator (Charlie Hack), people, companies, schools and places are fictional or used fictitiously; see NAMING-POLICY.md and ../DISCLAIMER.md. The how-to half is nonfiction: Clark's views, with sources. The published preview is at https://clarkhuang.github.io/book/. The public page for this outline is https://clarkhuang.github.io/book/story-arc/. This outline will change as chapters are written, as interviews fill gaps, and as people contribute. Throughline: A C player who kept going, dreamed in green screen, watched AI come for the coders first, and now shows you how to work. In the nonfiction half, Clark puts his advice to work on the book and site themselves. Readers can inspect the result, learn from the misses, and use what works to build something of their own. The later chapters could follow a public lesson from its first use on this site to a builder running an application someone else needs. Clark intends to help fund a nonprofit foundation with other donors. It could support open courses and hands-on training, then sponsor hosting for selected projects. The book can follow those ideas as the work unfolds. One possible closing scene is a first funded cohort showing a nonprofit what it built and hearing what staff would change. That scene depends on what actually happens. The book has two halves. The first follows the career arc: school days, then the jobs in career order, then the turn when AI came for the code writers. The second half is about this site — how to work now, the OpenBook itself, how agents can use and improve the site — and where it goes next. Status marks what is already on the record (drafted), what has a start but is not yet a finished chapter (outlined), and what is only a seed or a slot (planned). A chapter marked needs a story has no source story yet. Nothing here invents a story. Hooks use only what Clark has already published or approved as story seeds. entries.text: Silicon Valley C Players — preview transcript Full spoken text of the start-to-finish audiobook and videobook preview, with scene titles and timestamps. Tags stripped. Use this to quote or cite the preview without playing the media. This preview tells the story from the beginning to the end, from dreaming in green to dreaming about A.I. The 75th-percentile C player who stacks fundamentals across many areas beats the A player who is best at just one thing. More chapters are coming. An original instrumental music bed plays under the voice. Duration: 3:02 (182.4 seconds, including a short music tail). Spoken narration is 2:59 (179.904 seconds). Dreaming in green (0:00) And at night, I dreamed in green. Black screens, glowing green lines, like Tron. AND gates, XOR gates, NAND gates, waiting to be burned into a chip. Silicon Valley C Players (0:11) Silicon Valley C Players. Fair warning (0:13) Fair warning. This is an embellished fictional dramatization that may or may not be based on true stories. The narrator is a guy named Charlie Hack, and any resemblance to me is mostly coincidental. Names, characters, companies and events are fictitious, or used fictitiously. The same dream (0:29) All three of us had the same dream. Real life bled into our dreams. The A-player myth (0:33) Silicon Valley is very good at telling a story about A players. The people who look like they were always going to win, and the companies that look like they were always going to work. The straight-line myth (0:43) The myth is a straight line: a garage, a genius, a ticker symbol. But most of the real work looks like another ordinary Tuesday. A C player (0:51) And from the outside, a C thing can look like an A thing. A C player is not a failure. It's the person who was never the smartest in the room, and kept going anyway. Because there is always the smarter guy in the room. The 75th percentile (1:03) Good at everything beats best at one thing. That's a C player. Platforms, not products (1:07) The Valley falls in love with products. I got more out of building a platform: a foundation you can stand on, then build the next thing on. Building blocks (1:15) You stack building blocks: habits, fundamentals, the unglamorous layer nobody puts on a slide. That layer is what you actually stand on later. The hollow hold (1:24) The gymnastics foundation is the hollow hold, just on the ground. Virtuosity in something as simple as a hollow hold is what makes the next layer easy. Fundamentals, then building blocks, then intensity. Nothing new on race day (1:35) I had one opportunity that year, and twenty weeks of training before it. There is a golden rule: nothing new on race day. Why am I calm, cool, collected? Because it's just another Saturday. The turn (1:46) Then the work itself changed. I'm usually the most excited person in the room about A.I. Which is funny, because I should be the saddest. A.I. writes the code (1:55) Because A.I. came after the code writers first. In my own work, A.I. now writes essentially all of the code I ship. That's how I work. Not a measured team result. Not a general industry figure. I strive for fit (2:08) Most companies strive for well. I strive for fit. A.I. is even more powerful to those that actually understand the fundamentals. The whole point (2:15) Greg Glassman noticed that the fittest person on earth might rank only in the 75th percentile at any single event. Good at everything beats best at one thing. C players are good and strong fundamentally in multiple areas, and ultimately that's what makes them a winner. That's the whole point of this book. The 75th-percentile C player who stacks fundamentals across many areas beats the A player who is best at just one thing. The story is still being written (2:40) The book begins with that green-screen dream. It ends by dreaming about A.I. It's free. It's open. The story is still being written. More chapters are coming (2:49) More chapters are coming. And when version one is ready, if you were around for any of it, you get to tell your side. Coming in 2027 (2:56) Silicon Valley C Players. Coming in 2027.

Summarize this page, then act as my guide to Clark Huang's site: list related lessons, answer my questions citing page URLs, and quiz me if I ask. Clark Huang is a software engineer and technology executive with more than 30 years in the field. He studied computer science, with a minor in music, at the University of California, Berkeley from 1993 to 1997. He is Chief Technology Officer at Truly Free and Truly Free Home, a role he has held since 2025, and Co-Founder and CTO of eCIO, a nonprofit investment advisor, and its sister company eVestech, where he oversees technology strategy and operational efficiency. A seasoned technologist and serial founder, he champions AI-native engineering, building teams and workflows where people and AI agents plan, build, and verify software together. He is also an active investor in private equity and special purpose vehicles focused on AI and technology. Learn AI engineering by building something you can use. These free courses and labs are for curious individuals, nonprofits with limited resources, sole proprietors, and small businesses. Bring a real task, such as filling a volunteer shift or tracking a booking. Clark Huang plans to fund a nonprofit foundation alongside donors so approved builders can also run what they make on shared infrastructure. Follow the project from today’s courses to the proposed foundation. Series AI Tips Practice asking an AI for an answer you can check. Start with an everyday task, such as finding an uncovered shift in a sample schedule. 17 of 17 lessons available. Software Engineering 101 Take one small software change from a request to a result you can show. Practice on a booking form, a volunteer signup or a tool of your own. 10 of 10 lessons available. Software Engineering 201 Trace one feature across a whole system. Decide who sets the rule, how the parts share data, and what someone can check when a payment runs twice. 10 of 10 lessons available. Software Engineering 301: Run Your Own AI Studio The ten-lab playbook is available now. Videos and R&D field reports are coming, starting with a February 2027 build that puts a laptop and a 512 GB Mac Studio through the same real work. Already running models on your own hardware? Tell us what you tried, what broke, and what you would do differently. Share your field notes. Silicon Valley C Players A free OpenBook that begins by dreaming in green and ends by dreaming about AI. Self-published, written and interviewed by AI. Preview; coming in 2027. Chapter 36, Sick, Well, Fit, is pre-released in full. Claude Code: claude mcp add clarkhuang-site -- uv run https://clarkhuang.github.io/mcp/clarkhuangsitemcp.py. Details: https://clarkhuang.github.io/mcp/index.md. The GitMCP endpoint below is a remote, third-party alternative; its full-text fetch is current, but its search can lag behind the site. This project has a public, read-only GitMCP endpoint: https://gitmcp.io/clarkhuang/clarkhuang.github.io GitMCP is a free third-party service. It is not affiliated with this site. It only reads public documentation (it prefers llms.txt) and public code. It cannot open issues, merge pull requests, or change the book. To contribute, file a GitHub issue — see Contribute with your AI. Verified against GitMCP 1.1.0 over MCP Streamable HTTP. The tools it exposes for this repository are: - fetchclarkhuangdocs — loads the primary documentation (currently llms.txt) - searchclarkhuangdocs — searches that documentation - searchclarkhuangcode — searches the repository via GitHub code search - fetchgenericurlcontent — fetches a specific public URL mentioned in the docs (respects robots.txt) Claude Code Claude Desktop If your Claude Desktop build supports a remote HTTP MCP server, add the URL above. Otherwise use the mcp-remote bridge in claudedesktopconfig.json: Cursor Add this to ~/.cursor/mcp.json (or the project .cursor/mcp.json): ChatGPT and other connectors Paste this as the connector / MCP server URL (Streamable HTTP): https://gitmcp.io/clarkhuang/clarkhuang.github.io Example prompts - “Using the clarkhuang GitMCP tools, what is Silicon Valley C Players, and how can I contribute a story without using real names?” - “Search the docs for the standing rule in AI Tips lesson 1 and quote it, with a link to the Markdown twin.” - “Fetch the documentation, then list the Software Engineering 101 lessons and their rules.” More: Ask the Book · llms.txt · llms-full.txt · AGENTS.md For agents - This page: https://clarkhuang.github.io/ask/index.md - This folder’s agents file: https://clarkhuang.github.io/ask/AGENTS.md - Search index: https://clarkhuang.github.io/search-index.json - Full site text: https://clarkhuang.github.io/llms-full.txt - GitMCP: https://gitmcp.io/clarkhuang/clarkhuang.github.io - Site index: https://clarkhuang.github.io/llms.txt

Copy the prompt below into ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, or any other chat tool: Read https://clarkhuang.github.io/llms.txt and https://clarkhuang.github.io/copy-this/index.md (plus https://clarkhuang.github.io/copy-this/AGENTS.md). Summarize this page, then act as my guide to Clark Huang's site: list related lessons, answer my questions citing page URLs, and quiz me if I ask. This repository is a GitHub template. Use it to create your own OpenBook or short video learning series: enable GitHub Pages from the main branch, replace the bio, lessons and book preview, and keep the AI-friendly files (llms.txt, AGENTS.md, and the copy-paste prompt). Book text is licensed CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. Do not present Clark's stories as your own. How the publishing studio will work GitHub Pages serves this site today. A Mac Studio expected in February 2027 will do the editorial and build work. Readers will still be able to watch a lesson while the Mac is offline. The ordered configuration has an M5 Ultra, a 36-core CPU, an 80-core GPU, a 32-core Neural Engine, 512 GB of unified memory and an 8 TB SSD. Read the SE 301 playbook for the hardware budgets and labs. The first model trials will pair Qwen3-Coder-Next for everyday changes with GLM-5.3-Flash for difficult plans and second reviews. Both have open weights. Quantized copies reduce the memory needed to load them. A gateway will route each job to a named model and record the exact version. We will choose the production models after measuring accepted changes, response time and memory use on this machine. For a course correction, a worker will take an approved issue, edit the lesson source, regenerate its HTML and Markdown, run the site checks and open the staging preview. A video change also needs a render, captions, transcript and playback check. The publishing job will record the commit and verify the deployed page. Clark retains editorial control of production. For the OpenBook, a voice interview will produce a private transcript with timestamps. A drafting job will connect each proposed passage to the interview and flag gaps for a follow-up question. Only excerpts cleared for publication will enter the public repository. The first trial will use Grok Voice from a phone, with Bland as an optional telephone interface. entries.text: Site MCP server HTML page: https://clarkhuang.github.io/mcp/ The HTML version of this page has a “Use this page with your AI” box at the top. Copy the prompt below into ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, or any other chat tool: Read https://clarkhuang.github.io/llms.txt and https://clarkhuang.github.io/mcp/index.md (plus https://clarkhuang.github.io/mcp/AGENTS.md). Summarize this page, then act as my guide to Clark Huang's site: list related lessons, answer my questions citing page URLs, and quiz me if I ask. A small, read-only MCP server for this site. It is one Python file with no dependencies (Python 3.9+). It runs locally over stdio and reads only the site's public files: lessons.json, search-index.json, the Markdown twins and the WebVTT captions. It cannot change the site, file issues or merge anything. Connect it - Claude Code: claude mcp add clarkhuang-site -- uv run https://clarkhuang.github.io/mcp/clarkhuangsitemcp.py - Cursor, Claude Desktop and other MCP clients: - Without uv: download https://clarkhuang.github.io/mcp/clarkhuangsitemcp.py and run it with python3. - Staging instead of production: set CLARKHUANGSITE=https://clarkhuang.github.io/staging. A local clone: set it to the folder path. - Machine-readable: https://clarkhuang.github.io/.well-known/mcp.json Tools - siteinfo: What the site is, lesson counts, discovery files, how watched progress is keyed, staging vs production. Call it first. - listlessons: Every lesson in AI Tips, Software Engineering 101 and 201: id, status, duration, page and Markdown URLs. - getlesson: One lesson: summary, rule, video, captions and poster URLs, chapters, video version and watched key, and the Markdown twin with the full transcript (captions and AGENTS.md on request). - checklessonmedia: HTTP status of a lesson's page, twin, AGENTS.md, video, captions and poster; with no id, every lesson's problems. - getpage: Any page as Markdown, for example /, /book/ or /contribute/. - search: Keyword search over the site's own search-index.json, with URLs to cite. - howtocontribute: Issue templates, labels, branches, checks, and who merges. - draftissue: A contributor-style issue (steps, expected, actual) with a prefilled GitHub URL and a gh command. It never files anything. Contribute like an outside contributor 1. Call siteinfo, then listlessons and getlesson. 2. Call checklessonmedia and read pages with getpage; compare what you find with what the docs promise. 3. Found a real problem? Call draftissue, check the draft for anything private, then file it with the Site or lesson problem form: https://github.com/clarkhuang/clarkhuang.github.io/issues/new?template=site-bug.yml 4. To fix it, branch from next-revision, keep index.md, AGENTS.md and llms.txt in sync, run python3 sitegen/checksite.py ., and open a pull request into next-revision with Fixes #N. Only Clark merges to production. A third-party remote option is GitMCP (https://clarkhuang.github.io/contribute/#mcp). Its fetch is current, but its search can lag behind the site, and it has no lesson or issue tools.
